idiom_name: javax.crypto.SealedObject + Cipher sealing a serialized HashMap
implementation_notes: This is the source pattern's own realization: the transfer object keeps the protected name-value pairs in a HashMap, seals the serialized map with javax.crypto.SealedObject (its constructor takes a Serializable and a fully initialized Cipher) and drops the plaintext map, so any component that logs or forwards the object sees only the sealed form; consumers call getObject(Cipher) or getObject(Key) to recover it. What replaces the classic structure: SealedObject replaces the hand-rolled encryption of the data map while the JCE provider stack supplies the Cipher, and the masked-list variant remains for the case where only accidental exposure is the threat. Keep the sealed map to JDK value types (String, numbers, collections) so the payload stays safe to deserialize.
pitfalls: The Cipher must be fully initialized for sealing and re-initialized for decryption (DECRYPT_MODE) with the same algorithm, key and parameters; getObject(Cipher) otherwise throws IllegalBlockSizeException/BadPaddingException or an AEAD tag failure.

getObject(Key) deserializes the payload through ObjectInputStream, so a sealed object still opens Java's deserialization surface for whoever holds the key - keep the sealed map to JDK types and/or configure an ObjectInputFilter.

toString/hashCode and debugger views reflect over fields: clear the plaintext map after sealing, never hand out defensive copies of it, and override toString because IDE/Lombok-generated methods print every field.

Key distribution decides whether the pattern works at all: producers and consumers must share the symmetric key without exposing it to intermediaries, and the source pattern warns this may be harder than redesigning so the data need not pass through those components.
SealedObject is not transport security: it protects the payload from components and logs, not from a network eavesdropper who sees the sealed bytes - use TLS/Secure Pipe for the wire.

variants.name: Masked List Strategy (two maps, protected names omitted from output)
variants.idiom_name: two HashMaps + protected-name set + toString() suppression
variants.implementation_notes: The simpler strategy the source pattern documents: the transfer object keeps a list of protected element names, routes those values into a second map that toString(), the serializer and the audit view never render, and exposes them only through an explicit accessor. It prevents the accidental exposure that motivated the pattern (debug prints, audit logs, console output) at zero cryptographic cost, but any component holding the object can still read the values, so it must not be treated as a boundary against an untrusted intermediary. Keep it for closed trust models where the threat is logging, and move to the sealed variant when the route includes components that must not read the data.
pitfalls: Masking stops print/log exposure, not access: any component can call get("cardNumber"), so an untrusted intermediary still needs the sealed variant or a redesign that keeps the value out of its hands.

Every output path must be enrolled: Jackson/IDE toString, logback converters, exception messages and debugger views can still render the masked map when they walk fields instead of using the overridden toString.
The protected-name list is policy: adding a sensitive field without adding its name silently ships it in the clear, so the classification needs a test, not just the mechanism.
